hints: Look carefully at Table 3.1 and compare which organelles are missing in type A but abundant in type B - what kind of transport cell gives up its nucleus and most mitochondria to stay hollow for flow?
Think about what plasmodesmata actually are - tiny channels lined by plasma membrane that join the cytoplasm of two neighbouring cells.
Link that cytoplasmic connection to movement of sucrose - why would direct cell-to-cell diffusion be faster and more efficient than crossing membranes for loading into the transport tube?
walkthrough:
Use the Table to Identify the Cells**
Type A has cytoplasm and a cellulose wall but no nucleus, no ribosomes and few mitochondria. That is the classic sieve tube element - it is highly modified to offer least resistance to flow of assimilates. Type B with nucleus, many mitochondria and ribosomes is the companion cell that stays metabolically active to support it.

Remember What Plasmodesmata Do**
Plasmodesmata are pores through the walls where the plasma membranes and cytoplasm of the two cells are continuous. So sucrose does not have to cross a membrane and wall to get from companion cell to sieve tube element - it can stay in the cytoplasm all the way. This is called the symplast pathway.

Explain the Importance for Translocation**
Assimilates like sucrose are made in the leaf and actively loaded by companion cells. Direct cytoplasmic links allow rapid diffusion into the adjacent sieve tube element at the source for loading, and rapid diffusion out at the sink for unloading. That keeps mass flow in phloem fast and efficient.

Final answer: Cell type A: phloem sieve tube element. Plasmodesmata connect the cytoplasm of the sieve tube element to companion cell (type B) to form the symplast pathway, allowing rapid diffusion of sucrose / assimilates from cell to cell for efficient loading into / unloading from sieve tubes.

hints: Start with what is already given - callose is made from beta-glucose, so recall what monomer cellulose is also made from.
Look at Fig. 3.1 and trace the bond - find carbon 1 of one glucose joining to which carbon of the next glucose, then compare with the 1,4 bond you know in cellulose.
Think about how the position of the bond changes folding - a 1,4 link with flipped monomers gives a straight chain, so what shape must repeated same-orientation 1,3 links give?
Zoom in on the orientation of the CH2OH groups on C5 in Fig. 3.1 - are they flipped 180 degrees each time like in cellulose, or all pointing the same way?
walkthrough:
Identify the Monomer**
Both polysaccharides are polymers of glucose in the beta form. In Fig. 3.1 each ring has the OH on C1 and C2 in the positions characteristic of beta-glucose. So cellulose, like callose, uses beta-glucose.

Read the Glycosidic Bond from the Diagram**
In Fig. 3.1 follow the O link: C1 of one monomer joins to C3 of the next (labels 1C to 3C / 4C region). That is a 1,3 glycosidic bond. Cellulose is given as 1,4 glycosidic bond (C1 to C4).

Link Bond Position to Shape and Rotation**
In cellulose every alternate beta-glucose is rotated 180 degrees, allowing H-bonding into straight, linear microfibrils. In callose all monomers sit the same way up, so the 1,3 links cannot lie flat - the chain coils into a helix as stated in the table.

Complete the Comparison**
So the paired differences are: monomer same (beta-glucose), bond different (1,3 in callose vs 1,4 in cellulose), shape different (helix in callose vs straight in cellulose), orientation different (same way up in callose vs alternate rotated 180 degrees in cellulose).

Final answer: Cellulose molecule: monomer is beta-glucose; shape is straight / linear. Callose molecule: bond is 1,3 glycosidic bond; adjacent glucose molecules are orientated the same way up (not rotated).

hints: Recall that water is polar and forms hydrogen bonds - think of two types of attraction: water to water, and water to the hydrophilic xylem wall.
Consider what those attractions create inside a narrow dead xylem vessel - a continuous unbroken thread of water from roots to leaves.
Link evaporation at the leaf to upward movement - how does loss of vapour from mesophyll surfaces pull that whole column up?
walkthrough:
Separate Adhesion and Cohesion**
Hydrogen bonds form between water molecules (cohesion) and between water and the hydrophilic cellulose and lignin in the xylem vessel wall (adhesion). Adhesion helps support the column and prevents it collapsing away from the wall.

Build the Continuous Column**
Together cohesion and adhesion hold water as one continuous column up the xylem. Cohesion gives the column great tensile strength so it does not easily break when pulled.

Add Transpiration Pull**
Water evaporates from spongy mesophyll cell surfaces and diffuses out of the leaf as water vapour in transpiration. This creates tension / a water potential gradient that pulls the whole cohesive column upward from roots to leaves.

Final answer: Hydrogen bonding causes adhesion of water to cellulose / hydrophilic lignin in xylem walls and cohesion between water molecules, forming a continuous water column that is pulled up by transpiration pull / tension created by evaporation from leaves.

hints: Focus on what must happen to hydrogen bonds for liquid water to become vapour - bonds must be broken, and breaking bonds needs energy.
Think about where that heat energy comes from - if the evaporating water takes heat from the leaf surface, what happens to leaf temperature?
walkthrough:
Why Evaporation Needs Energy**
Liquid water is held together by many hydrogen bonds. To change state to vapour these bonds must be broken. Breaking bonds absorbs a large amount of energy, which is why water has a high latent heat of vaporisation.

Explain the Cooling Effect**
During transpiration the energy comes as heat from the leaf cells and the water film. When the highest-energy water molecules escape as vapour they carry that heat away, leaving the leaf with less heat energy and therefore cooler.
Final answer: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules must break for evaporation, which requires heat / energy. This heat is taken from the leaf, so loss of heat cools the leaf.
